Rise above the glare. Leave the look-down behind.

Avenger220

A research-led redesign of the Avenger 220 instrument cluster, moving ride data from the fuel tank into the rider's line of sight.

Designer
Deepanshi Nagarwal
Scope
UX research, IA, UI, prototype
Method
Mixed-method · 194-rider survey
Tools
Figma, Figma Make, hand sketch
01 The problem

Iconic bike.
Dated cockpit.

The Avenger is Bajaj's cruiser: relaxed ergonomics, chrome, long-distance comfort. Its cluster never kept up. Critical data sits small, split between headlamp and tank, and fades in glare.

1Tank console forces a look-downEyes leave the road to check fuel and indicators.
2LCD washes out in sunChrome reflects glare straight back at the rider.
3No live ride dataNo instant mileage, average speed or trip analytics.
4No connectivityNo Bluetooth or navigation; a phone mount fills the gap.
5Scattered iconsNo grouping logic for warnings vs. status.
Stage 1EmpathizeLiterature review and benchmark audit of 14 Indian and global clusters.
Stage 2ResearchQuestionnaire to 194 two-wheeler riders; feature-importance and usage analysis.
Stage 3DefinePersona, empathy map, storyboard, 9 How-Might-We questions, ISO 6727 / AIS-126 constraints.
Stage 4Ideate4 directions, each hand-sketched then built in Figma.
Stage 5PrototypeClickable Figma Make prototype, day/night states, in-context mockups.
02 What 194 riders told us

Read in a
heartbeat.

A shared class questionnaire covered rider profile, current dashboard use and preferences. The sample skews experienced and daily, exactly the people who notice a bad cluster.

194Riders surveyed
79%Experienced riders
70%Ride daily
70%Two-wheeler is primary vehicle
Q · Which elements do you check most while riding?

Two things get checked by nearly everyone

InsightSpeed and fuel are near-universal glances (~87% each); everything else is checked by fewer than half. The cluster should give these two a tier of their own.

n = 194 · digital-dashboard users · % of respondents

Q · How important is each feature? (1–5)

Fuel and speed lead; notifications trail

InsightNavigation has the widest spread (2–5): riders split on it. That argues for navigation as an optional view, not a permanent fixture.

Dot = median, bar = middle 50% (Q1–Q3). Values read from the survey box plot.

Q · How do you feel about smart connected features?

The middle 40% is the market

44%
40%
17%
Enthusiasts Neutral Avoiders

InsightDesigning for enthusiasts plus neutrals covers 84% of riders. Smart features must be easy enough to convert the neutral middle, while a clean default screen keeps the 17% comfortable.

Shares as reported in the analysis (rounded; total 101%).

Item–total correlation · how strongly each feature tracks overall dashboard engagement

Engaged riders care about modes, navigation and service

InsightAll eight items pass the 0.3 reliability threshold, so the feature set hangs together. Riding modes, navigation and service reminders correlate most with engagement, so they earned a place in the IA as secondary screens.

Approximate values read from the analysis chart (≈ ±0.01). Dashed line = 0.3 minimum threshold.

03 Benchmark

14 clusters,
one gap.

From Hero commuters and Royal Enfield to Ola's touchscreen and superbike TFTs. Indian clusters either stay analogue and sparse or go full digital and busy. A cruiser has room in between.

Positioning map · qualitative

Where the redesign sits

GapDigital and rich enough for ride data and pairing, but calmer than a superbike TFT. The cruiser keeps a classic silhouette.

Placement is a design judgement from the benchmark audit, not a measurement.

05 Storyboard

One morning
ride.

Six frames from Aftab's day show where the current cluster fails him. The near-miss in frame 5 is the moment the whole redesign is built around.

?!?!!?
!?!!?!
Move the data
to the line of sight.

Every frame traces back to two failures: position (tank vs. headlamp) and legibility (glare, reflection, size). The redesign answers both.

Emotion journey across the six frames

Today's ride dips hardest at the look-down; the redesign targets a flat line

Qualitative scale (−2 stressed to +2 at ease), mapped from the storyboard and empathy map. The target line is design intent, not test data.

06 From pain to principle

Every pain,
a decision.

Nine How-Might-We questions were folded into a traceability matrix, so each design move points back to evidence.

Pain pointEvidenceHow might we…Design response
Fuel and tell-tales on the tank force a look-downStoryboard 04–05 · 85.6% check fuel…keep critical data in the line of sight?Single cluster in the headlamp nacelle; fuel bar, indicators and warnings all move up from the tank.
LCD unreadable in sunlightPersona · Storyboard 03, 06…stay visible in glare and at night?High-contrast ice-cyan backlight; Day / Night / Auto modes with a brightness slider; amber night palette.
Speed hard to read at a glance88.7% check speed most…set a clear hierarchy?Speed is the largest element on screen (7-segment, 60 × 20 mm), top-centre.
No live ride dataPersona goals · empathy "Says"…add data without overload?One quiet row for average speed and odometer under the RPM read-out.
No pairing or navigation44% enthusiasts · nav spread 2–5…use modern display tech?Bluetooth pairing via the Bajaj app; navigation as an optional full-screen view with speed pinned.
Scattered icons, tiny buttonsPersona pain points · ISO 6727…cut cognitive load?Tell-tales grouped on two arcs by severity colour; a single settings entry point.
Service dates forgottenService reminders r ≈ 0.66…support ownership, not just riding?Maintenance alert tell-tale plus a servicing-reminder screen.
07 Constraints

Built to
the rulebook.

ISO 6727:2021 symbols and AIS-126 tell-tale rules set the colour logic, placement and fail-safe behaviour. Colour encodes severity; position encodes type.

Red · stopBattery, oil pressure, coolant temperature, engine, ABS. Lit continuously while a fault is active.
Amber · cautionLow fuel, maintenance alert. Low fuel escalates to a blinking red fuel bar.
Green · statusLeft / right indicators, neutral. Large flanking arrows at the base.
Blue · beamHigh beam, top of the left arc, where ISO convention puts it.
08 Ideation

Four
directions.

Each idea went from pencil to Figma and was placed on the actual Avenger nacelle to judge fit and glanceability, not just looks.

01 · Chrome analogueRound, chrome-edged needle gauge with gear and RPM sub-dials.Strong retro fit. A needle takes longer to read than a number, and leaves little room for connectivity.
02 · Retro TFTDark round TFT with an arc tachometer and a central speed number.Modern, but dense. Dark ground loses contrast in daylight glare.
03 · Shield LCD SelectedShield-shaped, bright LCD with a stacked hierarchy and handlebar joystick controls.Largest speed read-out, bright ground for sunlight, tell-tales on two arcs. Fits the nacelle.
04 · Split circleCircular LCD split by a vertical fuel / RPM bar.Distinctive, but splits speed and RPM into equal halves, flattening the hierarchy.
09 Information architecture

Two taps,
max.

Every secondary screen is reachable in two inputs from the main display, and every one ends with a single "Return to dashboard" action.

Main dashboard display
BluetoothSearch devicePairing via Bajaj appConnection successfulBack to main display
NavigationMap navigationRoute timeDistanceEstimated arrival
SettingsMode: Standard / Sport / Eco / TourDisplay: Day / Night / Auto, brightnessAbout: maintenance alerts
IndicatorsHigh beamLeft / right indicatorFuel levelLow fuel → blink red
10 Final design

Speed first.
Then everything else.

A shield-shaped LCD on an ice-cyan ground. Information stacks top to bottom in the order riders check it, with tell-tales held on the frame so the screen stays calm.

Tier 1 · glanceSpeed + gearLargest 7-segment digits, gear and ride mode beside them. Readable in under a second.
Tier 2 · scanRPM + ride dataTachometer, then a quiet row of average speed and odometer.
Tier 3 · peripheryTell-tales + fuelSeverity-coloured icons on two arcs; fuel bar, clock and Bluetooth at the base.
Check rate vs. screen area · does space follow attention?

Speed is sized right. Fuel is under-sized for how often it's checked.

Next iterationFuel is checked almost as often as speed (85.6% vs 88.7%) but gets a sixth of the area. Enlarging the fuel bar, or adding range in km beside it, would align space with attention.

Area = specified element dimensions (speed 60 × 20 mm, fuel bar 20 × 10 mm, odometer 30 × 8 mm). The odometer was not asked about in the survey.

11 Screen states

One frame,
six states.

The tell-tale arcs, fuel bar and clock stay fixed across every state, so the rider never loses safety-critical information while browsing a menu.

SolvedAll ride-critical data now lives in one headlamp cluster, in the line of sight. The tank look-down from frame 5 is designed out.
ProvedHierarchy follows the survey: the 88.7% item is the biggest; the 29% item is a peripheral icon. Standards-compliant tell-tales by severity.
